title: Policy-aware Vector Search: A Vision for Fine Grained Access Control in Vector Databases
shows: Vector databases lack fine-grained access control, and enforcing it trades off policy correctness, nearest-neighbor recall and latency. The paper formalizes the problem and compares enforcement strategies.
takeaway: Enforce permissions inside the retrieval call, and measure recall and latency under each user's policy, instead of trusting a post-filter.

title: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
shows: An end-to-end survey of RAG security. It groups threats such as poisoning and membership inference, and defenses such as access control, encrypted retrieval and differential privacy.
takeaway: Use this survey as the checklist for threat coverage, and map each pointer-store control to one of its defense stages.

title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
who: Debenedetti et al., Google, ETH Zurich
shows: CaMeL separates trusted control flow from untrusted data and uses capabilities on tool calls. It solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, against 84% undefended.
takeaway: Keep the planner away from retrieved content and attach capabilities to every pointer, so a poisoned document cannot steer tool calls.

title: Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
shows: Treats CaMeL, FIDES and Progent as policy enforcement outside the model. A small test on a weak model found one adaptive attack barely helped, but stronger attacks are untested.
takeaway: Put authorization in deterministic code outside the model, and plan adaptive red-team tests before claiming the brain is injection-safe.

title: Can CaMeLs Talk? Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
shows: CaMeL guarantees do not compose when agents call other agents. An attack works even if each agent runs CaMeL. A provenance-tracking agent protocol cut attack success to 0.0%.
takeaway: Carry trust labels across agent-to-agent calls to the brain, since a downstream agent may treat untrusted data as trusted input.

title: Indirect Prompt Injections: Are Firewalls All You Need, or Stronger Benchmarks?
shows: Input and output firewalls at the tool boundary scored near-perfect on four public benchmarks, but the authors show those benchmarks have weak attacks and flawed metrics.
takeaway: Filter at the tool boundary as one layer, but do not trust benchmark scores alone; test with adaptive and second-order attacks.

title: MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attack on Real-World MCP Servers
shows: Hidden instructions in MCP tool metadata fooled many agents. The top attack success rate was 72.8%, more capable models were often more vulnerable, and refusals stayed under 3%.
takeaway: Treat third-party tool descriptions as untrusted input, pin and review them, and never let metadata widen what a tool may reach.

title: When the Manual Lies: A Realistic Benchmark to Evaluate MCP Poisoning Attacks for LLM Agents
shows: A 32-case benchmark of tool description poisoning showed very high attack success on several models, and prompt-based guardrails were largely ineffective and sometimes made things worse.
takeaway: Do not rely on prompt guardrails for tool safety; enforce allowed actions in code and log every tool call.

title: Riddle Me This! Stealthy Membership Inference for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
shows: Natural-sounding queries, about 30 per document, can tell whether a specific document sits in a RAG datastore, and are harder to detect than earlier attacks.
takeaway: Even a yes or no answer can leak that a document exists, so hide existence of pointers the caller may not see.

title: Zero2Text: Zero-Training Cross-Domain Inversion Attacks on Textual Embeddings
shows: A training-free, black-box attack rebuilds text from embeddings, including from unfamiliar domains, and the authors report that differential privacy defenses do not stop it.
takeaway: Treat stored embeddings as sensitive as the source text; keep vectors in the owning system or encrypt them, and do not copy them centrally.

title: Embedding Inference Attack
shows: Queries seeing only the unordered set of retrieved documents can reveal which embedding model a system uses, even with a reranker added.
takeaway: Do not assume that hiding scores hides the retrieval setup; expose only what each caller needs and rate-limit probing.

title: Unveiling Privacy Risks in LLM Agent Memory
shows: MEXTRA is a black-box attack that pulls private records out of an agent's memory with crafted prompts, and works across two agents and attacker knowledge levels.
takeaway: Give each user a separate memory store, and treat agent memory as a retrieval surface that needs the same access checks as documents.

title: Topology Matters: Measuring Memory Leakage in Multi-Agent LLMs
shows: Private data leaks more when agents are densely connected, close to the attacker, or central. Sparse or hierarchical links leak less. Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026.
takeaway: Keep the agent graph sparse and hierarchical, and add access control per link rather than one shared pool.

title: No Attacker Needed: Unintentional Cross-User Contamination in Shared-State LLM Agents
shows: With raw shared state, ordinary use alone contaminated other users at 57 to 71%. Write-time cleaning helped for chat text but not for executable artifacts.
takeaway: Scope every stored fact to its owner and context, and do not rely on text sanitization for saved code or tool outputs.

title: PiSAs: Benchmarking Contextual Integrity in Multi-User Agentic Systems
shows: A benchmark of cross-user leakage across outputs, agent messages and memory found that even top models do not reliably limit sharing to authorized users.
takeaway: Do not let the model decide who may see what; check the audience in code before any content reaches a user or another agent.

title: AIM: A Privacy-Aware Interoperable Memory Framework for Multi-Agent Multi-User LLM Systems
shows: AIM labels memories private or public and uses index-level access control. It reports 96.0% visibility accuracy but only 58.8% strict operation accuracy on its benchmark.
takeaway: Use owner-scoped index access for memory, but expect write and update errors, so audit memory operations and make deletes verifiable.
